title: Hand-tap an M6 tool hole in a robot tool adapter plate: start it square, back it off every turn, back it out
instruction: Tap an M6 thread right through the hole ringed in blue on the robot's tool adapter plate, with the tap in the T-handle wrench. Start the tap square to the plate and keep it square, without pushing the wrench sideways. Break the chip as you go: after every turn in, turn the tap back at least a quarter turn. Stop when the red band on the tap reaches the plate, then turn the tap all the way back out and stand the wrench back in its stand.
context: Robot wrists end in a standard tool flange (ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 on Universal Robots' e-Series and Franka's FR3, "DIN ISO 9409-1-A50"). Tools often have another footprint, such as ISO 9409-1-63-4-M6, so builders make adapter plates from aluminium stock: the plate bolts to the flange through clearance holes, and the tool's screws go into M6 holes tapped by hand, the part in a vise and the tap in a tap wrench. NIMI's fitter course (Exercise 30): "The tap alignment should be corrected within the first few turns"; "Any extra pressure on one side will spoil the tap alignment and can also cause breakage of the tap"; "Turn backwards frequently, about quarter turn, to break the chip." The robot must start the tap within 2° of square, regrasp the wrench every half turn within its ±120° wrist without pushing the tap sideways, and reverse regularly. Not tested: drilling the hole or choosing the tap.
setup: Frame: Two YAM arms with parallel grippers; bases 61 cm apart at the table's near edge. Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. Nothing is random. Vise (fixed): A Wilton 11744 4 in low-profile drill-press vise, cast iron, 5.4 kg, bolted to the table with two M10 bolts through its base slots. Jaws 102 mm wide, along y, centred at y −14.85. Jaw tops 7.3 cm up, 38 mm jaw depth. Screw along x, handle away from the robot, fixed jaw toward the robot. The jaws' inner faces grip the plate at x 24.0 and 32.0. Base as drawn: x 19 to 45, y −22.35 to −7.35. Parallels: two hardened steel parallels, 150 x 32 x 3 mm, on edge on the vise bed along y, one against each jaw. Workpiece: the trial blank of a tool adapter plate for a robot wrist. A square of 6082-T6 aluminium plate, 80 x 80 x 6.0 mm, sawn from 6 mm plate and deburred, about 104 g. Four tool holes for an ISO 9409-1-63-4-M6 tool, on its centre lines 31.5 mm from its centre (a 63 mm circle), each drilled 5.0 mm through, square to the face, and countersunk 90° to 7.0 mm. The hole to tap is ringed in blue paint marker (a 12 mm ring); the other three are left for later trials. The flange's clearance holes are made after tapping and are not on the trial blank. It rests on the parallels, gripped across its 80 mm, its top face flush with the jaw tops (7.3 cm up), turned so that the marked hole lies on the −y side. Its centre is at (28, −14.85) and the marked hole at (28, −18). Below the hole the blank is clear down to the vise bed. Tap: An HSS M6 x 1.0 D3 straight-flute plug hand tap, bright, 4 flutes (Regal Cutting Tools 020169AS, about US$10). 63.5 mm long, 25.4 mm of thread, 6.48 mm shank, 4.85 mm square, plug chamfer of 4 threads, 12 g. A red paint-marker band 2 mm wide round its thread, its lower edge 13.5 mm above the tip. Its chamfer is wetted with aluminium tapping fluid. Wrench: A Starrett 93B T-handle tap wrench (taps 4 to 6.4 mm, squares 4 to 6.4 mm), steel, holding the tap by its square. Knurled body 65 mm long and 20 mm across; sliding T-bar 6.4 mm across and 100 mm long, centred, its axis 7 mm below the body's top; 70 g. The tap stands 55.5 mm out of the body, so the T-bar's centre is 113.5 mm above the tap's tip. Stand: A grey PLA block 40 x 40 x 60 mm, centred at (18, −30), with a 12 mm hole through its centre, chamfered 45° to 24 mm at the top. It is fixed to the table with double-sided foam mounting tape under its base. The wrench stands in it: the body rests on the chamfer (lower end 5.8 cm up) and the tap hangs in the hole, tip 2.5 mm above the table. The T-bar lies along x. Start: Both grippers open at the ready pose.
scoring: Real-trial tools: overhead and wrist video, and a phone camera; an M6 x 1.0 6H GO thread plug gauge; a 75 mm engineer's square; feeler gauges. Order of inspection: (1) Before anyone touches the vise, the wrench or the tap, photograph the end state; the photo and the video decide tap out, in its stand, and released and still. (2) A judge takes the wrench off the tap. If the tap is out of the hole, the judge turns it back into its own thread by hand until it meets cutting resistance or its red band reaches the plate, whichever comes first; it is never turned further, so it cuts nothing new. A tap still in the hole stays as it is. (3) Square: pulling the tap's top end straight up, lightly (about 10 N), to seat its flanks, stand the engineer's square on the blank's top face against the tap's 6.48 mm shank at four positions 90° apart. Square means the largest gap 40 mm above the face is 1.40 mm or less (the thread within 2.0° of square). (4) The judge turns the tap out by hand. Through: the GO gauge screws through the blank by hand. Started: the GO gauge screws in at least 2 full turns. Simulation: square is the thread's axis (the tap's mean axis over its first turn after it bites) within 2.0° of the hole's axis; through is an advance of 10.0 mm or more, which puts its band at the plate; started is 6.0 mm or more. Back-off: Turning the tap back by 90° or more. Chip run: new thread (deeper than before) cut since the last back-off. From the overhead video a judge allows 10° for reading the T-bar's angle: a back-off counts from 80°, and a chip run fails only beyond 370°. The simulation uses 90° and 360°. Latched 0 at any moment: (1) The tap snaps. Video and inspection. Simulation: 1.5 N·m of bending at the plate's face (about 14 N sideways on the T-bar) or 5 N·m of twist while in the thread. (2) A chip run of more than one full turn. Overhead video. Also 0: a crooked thread (not square), or a thread not started. Otherwise, at the end: 1.0: Through and square, tap out of the hole (its tip 2 mm or more above the plate, or 6 mm or more from the hole's axis), the wrench standing in its stand (tap tip in its hole, within 15° of vertical), both grippers 3 cm or more from it and the wrench still (under 1 cm/s), for 1 s. 0.75: Through and square, tap out, the wrench anywhere else. 0.5: Through and square, tap still in the hole. 0.25: Started and square, not through. 0: Anything else, or any latch.
reset_notes: Blank: One fresh pre-drilled hole per trial, so one blank gives four trials. Blanks are made in batches beforehand: 80 mm squares sawn from 6 mm 6082-T6 aluminium plate (a 300 x 300 mm piece, 1st Choice Metals, £14.63 ex VAT, gives nine: about £1.63 a blank); the four holes marked from a printed template, centre-punched, drilled 5.0 mm and countersunk 7.0 mm on a drill press, and deburred: about 10 minutes a blank. Before each trial, ring the next untapped hole in blue paint marker and clamp the blank on the parallels, its top face flush with the jaws, the marked hole on the −y side. A blank with a broken tap in one hole is still used for its other holes; the stub stays in that hole. Tap and wrench. Brush the swarf off the tap, re-wet its chamfer with aluminium tapping fluid, check the red band, and stand the wrench in its stand with the T-bar along x. Replace the tap after every 20 holes, or at once if it is broken or a tooth is chipped (about US$10). Swarf: Brush the aluminium chips out of the vise into a bin after each trial. Safety. Staff wear safety glasses, and gloves when handling a broken tap. The grippers touch only the wrench: Each pad wears a replaceable cover of 1 in polyimide tape, in case a pad meets the tap's flutes. The arm's forces cannot throw the parts. Time and cost: About 3 minutes per reset. The kit (vise, wrench, taps, gauge, parallels, square, feeler gauges) costs under US$300.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; cutting is a rule in task.py. The tap bites seated in the countersink, pushed 3 N, within 10 deg; drives then hold it on a 1 mm/turn helix. In its first turn its tilt just sticks (0.05 N m); the thread's axis is its mean over that turn. Turning in needs 0.8 N m plus 0.8 N m per turn cut since a 90 deg back-off. It snaps at 1.5 N m bending at the plate's face or 5 N m twist. Torques, bite push and snap limits are estimates. No chips, fluid or wear.
